note: Standing nestor, jeles and willow-mcp up together for the first time. Three of the joins between them were broken and none of the three announced it — each package's own half was correct, and nothing had ever exercised the join. The decisions worth keeping are about seats and about what a passing check is allowed to mean.

decisions.question: Which environment variable names the seat Nestor's FRANK mirror calls as?
decisions.commitment: NESTOR_FRANK_APP_ID, read before WILLOW_APP_ID rather than instead of it.
decisions.why: WILLOW_APP_ID is client-scoped — it means 'the seat this client is driving', one value per shell, inherited by everything in the process that falls back to it. Read first, it silently re-seated the forwarder: a shell set up for the orchestrator made Nestor call frank_append as `willow`, which willow-mcp refuses outright because that seat demands a human-orchestrator host. So a correctly configured Nestor stopped mirroring the instant an operator sourced a fleet environment, and the only place that said so was the call site. The failure mode is the argument for the fix: a package must not take its identity from a variable another package owns. Reading WILLOW_APP_ID second rather than dropping it keeps every seat that is named only that way working, so this is precedence, not removal — and the collision was found by writing the bug into the fleet env file and watching the seam go red, not by reasoning about it.

decisions.question: Is Nestor a specialist in willow-mcp's registry, or an operator-local seat?
decisions.commitment: Operator-local. Its manifest is written to $WILLOW_HOME/mcp_apps/nestor/ by the stand-up script and never compiled from the registry.
decisions.why: willow-mcp's specialist registry describes dispatchable agents with personas — Hanuman builds, Loki audits, Jeles retrieves. Nestor is not one of those; it is a package that mirrors a hash-chained ledger into a shared one. Seeding it as a specialist would put a persona-shaped hole in a registry that every fleet operator inherits, to serve one integration. compile_manifests only walks registry rows, so a hand-written directory beside them is left alone on every recompile — the mechanism for exactly this case already existed and did not need changing. The grant is frank_write (mirror the ledger), fleet_read (verify the chain) and gap_read (import the backlog); deliberately not gap_write and not gap_promote, because Nestor reads what the fleet does not know and does not answer for it.

decisions.question: What is a seam check allowed to assert about the nugget bridge?
decisions.commitment: Not that it imports. That nothing arrived sealed — and the check fails if anything did.
decisions.why: The bridge's entire claim is that an unsigned assertion does not cross as a seal: jeles is scrupulous about verified_by and every one of its protections is a good decision and none of them is a check, so every nugget arrives as a draft. A test that imports the module and confirms it has a MATCHER asserts nothing about that. The check therefore bridges real nuggets into a throwaway store and fails on a non-zero `sealed` count or any sealed row left behind — the same assertion the recipe's docstring makes in prose. It also installs and removes the custom matcher around the call, because the surface still cannot be told about one; that limitation is §6.40 and this work does not fix it, so the check runs the way the docstring's warning says is the only correct way.

decisions.question: What makes a fleet seam trustworthy enough to call 'stood up'?
decisions.commitment: Data written through the real path — the gate, the shared SQLite file, the hash chain — never an import that resolves.
decisions.why: All three broken joins passed an import-level reading. jeles imported, willow-mcp imported, the store paths looked right in both. The gap forward was denied by a manifest ACL, the FRANK append hit a table that did not exist, and the two stores were two different files whenever WILLOW_STORE_ROOT was unset. Every one of those needed a write to surface, and two of them needed a *read back through the other package* — a round trip inside one package proves nothing about the other. The corollary that cost the most to learn: a seam that cannot be reached must report SKIP, not PASS. Postgres absent is a smaller claim than FRANK working, and reporting the smaller claim as the larger one is how a stand-up certifies a fleet that is half up.
